payload.scope: People made cepstral-magnitude as a derived representation of spectral magnitude in the quefrency domain for analysis and inversion.

definition.body: A cepstral-magnitude is the magnitude component of cepstral coefficients after inverse Fourier transform of log-magnitude spectrum, representing the envelope-like contribution of the signal in quefrency domain. Parameters: quefrency index, magnitude of cepstral coefficient, liftering window, frame length. Persistence mechanism: computed in speech analysis toolkits, stored in feature extraction pipelines, and used in phase retrieval algorithms. e.g.: the magnitude of the real cepstrum of a speech frame extracted in Kaldi for MFCC computation; the cepstral magnitude used in Griffin-Lim iteration for magnitude spectrogram inversion; the cepstral magnitude envelope used in homomorphic deconvolution of speech | not: cepstral-phase (the angular component, not magnitude); power spectrum (frequency domain magnitude squared, not quefrency domain) [formal: magnitudo cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: companding
payload.scope: People made companding to fit a signal's wide dynamic range into a fixed number of bits per sample for transmission and recording.

definition.body: Companding is a compress-expand procedure that fits a wide dynamic range signal into a fixed number of bits per sample. The compressor applies a piecewise nonlinearity to the input so that small amplitudes receive fine quantization steps and large amplitudes receive coarse ones; a uniform quantizer then maps the compressed value to a level; an expander inverts the nonlinearity at the receiver to reconstruct a linear output. Parameters: (1) the nonlinearity shape - the mu-law of ITU-T G.711 or the a-law of ITU-T G.711; (2) the number of quantization bits, 8 in the standard telephony case; (3) the sample rate. Persistence mechanism: standardized in the ITU-T G.711 and G.712 recommendations, deployed in the public switched telephone network (E1 and T1 line systems), described in DSP and telephony textbooks, and implemented in telephony hardware and software codecs. e.g.: the a-law 8-bit 3.1 kHz telephone channel of the ITU-T G.711 recommendation on E1 lines; the mu-law 8-bit channel of ITU-T G.711 on T1 lines; the G.712 32 kbit/s log-law speech coding used on the ISDN basic rate interface | not: linear 8-bit PCM (no compression, uniform steps across the full range); delta modulation (predictive coding, not compress-expand); a dynamic-range compressor for audio mixing (a loudness shaping device, not a quantizer nonlinearity) [formal: compressio expansio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pulse-code-modulation
payload.scope: People made pulse-code-modulation to represent a continuous signal exactly enough for digital storage and transmission by sampling it at regular instants and quantizing each sample to a finite set of levels.

definition.body: Pulse-code-modulation (PCM) is a human-made procedure that represents a continuous signal in digital form by three stages. Sampling takes instantaneous values of the signal at a fixed sampling rate, typically above twice its highest frequency; quantization maps each sample to the nearest of a finite set of levels; encoding transmits the index of each level as a binary code word of a fixed number of bits. Parameters: (1) the sampling rate, 3.1 kHz in the standard telephony case; (2) the number of quantization bits per sample, 8 in the standard case; (3) the quantization law, uniform (linear) or logarithmic (the mu-law or a-law of companding). Persistence mechanism: standardized in the ITU-T G.711 recommendations, deployed in the public switched telephone network and in digital audio (the compact disc at 44.1 kHz with 16 bits), described in DSP textbooks, and implemented in every audio interface and telephony card. e.g.: the 64 kbit/s 3.1 kHz 8-bit channel of the ITU-T G.711 recommendation; the 44.1 kHz 16-bit compact disc audio track of the Red Book standard; the 8 kHz 14-bit G.703 PCM line used in digital telephone trunking | not: delta modulation (codes changes between samples, not sample values); ADPCM (adaptive step-size differential coding, a different prediction stage); a digital audio file format (a container, not the sampling-quantization procedure) [formal: modulatio impulsuum codicis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Pulse-code-modulation (PCM) is a human-made procedure that represents a continuous signal in digital form by three stages. Sampling takes instantaneous values of the signal at a fixed sampling rate, typically above twice its highest frequency; quantization maps each sample to the nearest of a finite set of levels; encoding transmits the index of each level as a binary code word of a fixed number of bits. Parameters: (1) the sampling rate, 3.1 kHz in the standard telephony case; (2) the number of quantization bits per sample, 8 in the standard case; (3) the quantization law, uniform (linear) or logarithmic (the mu-law or a-law of companding). Persistence mechanism: standardized in the ITU-T G.711 recommendations, deployed in the public switched telephone network and in digital audio (the compact disc at 44.1 kHz with 16 bits), described in DSP textbooks, and implemented in every audio interface and telephony card. e.g.: the 64 kbit/s 3.1 kHz 8-bit channel of the ITU-T G.711 recommendation; the 44.1 kHz 16-bit compact disc audio track of the Red Book standard; the 8 kHz 14-bit G.703 PCM line used in digital telephone trunking | not: delta modulation (codes changes between samples, not sample values); ADPCM (adaptive step-size differential coding, a different prediction stage); a digital audio file format (a container, not the sampling-quantization procedure) [formal: modulatio impulsuum codicis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.note: Named-operand, Law 8b removal test stated with result. PCM's own carve defines three stages and names stage 2: 'quantization maps each sample to the nearest of a finite set of levels'. Removing the quantization step (the mapping of sample values to a discrete level set) leaves sampling and the encoding of a continuous value that no finite bit pattern can carry - the procedure stops operating, it does not merely stop being sayable. The quantizer is a direct stage of PCM's own procedure, not nested in a sub-procedure. Direction dependent->needed. Sense pinned to the accepted quantization carve: 'mapping continuous or high-precision numerical values to a discrete, lower-precision representation' - the uniform level set of a PCM channel is exactly that mapping. payload.name: adaptive-filter
payload.scope: People made adaptive filters to track and cancel time-varying interference and equalize channels without manual tuning.

definition.body: Adaptive filter is a human-made signal processing structure that updates its coefficients in response to input data to minimize an error criterion. Parameters: adaptation algorithm (LMS, NLMS, RLS), step size or forgetting factor, filter order (tap count), input signal statistics. Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries, audio equalizers, echo cancellers, and wireless modem chips, and taught in adaptive signal processing courses. e.g.: NLMS adaptive echo canceller in ITU-T G.168; RLS adaptive beamformer in GSM base station receiver; LMS lattice adaptive noise canceller in GNU Radio; adaptive equalizer in ADSL modem | not: fixed FIR filter with static coefficients; Kalman filter for state estimation with process and measurement noise models [formal: filtrum adaptivum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: source-filter
payload.scope: People made the source-filter model to describe speech production as an excitation source driving a vocal tract filter, enabling separation of vocal fold vibrations from tract shape for analysis and synthesis.

definition.body: The source-filter model is a human-made decomposition of speech production into two independent subsystems. The source produces a quasi-periodic excitation signal characterized by fundamental frequency (pitch), source spectrum (harmonic structure), and voicing state (voiced/voiceless). The filter represents the vocal tract as an acoustic tube whose shape determines resonance frequencies (formants) and bandwidths. The model assumes independence between source and filter during steady-state production, so the output spectrum equals the product of source spectrum and filter transfer function. Parameters: (1) fundamental frequency F0, typically 80-500 Hz; (2) number of formant frequencies F1, F2, F3, F4; (3) formant bandwidths; (4) voicing flag; (5) glottal pulse shape (Rosenberg, LF model). Persistence mechanism: taught in speech processing textbooks, implemented in speech analysis tools (Praat, HTK, Kaldi), encoded in speech coding standards (G.723.1, AMR), and used in formant synthesis vocoders. e.g.: formant parameters in the Klatt synthesizer of CSL's KLP language; source-filter analysis in Praat by Boersma and Weenik; the LPC-derived source-filter decomposition in Kaldi's speech processing pipeline; formant-based vowel classification in phonetics research by Peter Ladefoged | not: acoustic resonance of a non-speech tube (a physical phenomenon, not the analytical model); the source-filter model applied to vocal tract imaging (a medical imaging task, not the production model itself) [formal: Fons-filtri | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: code-excited-linear-prediction
payload.scope: People made code-excited linear prediction to achieve high-quality speech coding at low bit rates by using a codebook of excitation patterns instead of a simple pitch residual, enabling full-rate and half-rate mobile telephone speech coding.

definition.body: Code-excited linear prediction (CELP) is a human-made speech coding technique that synthesizes natural-sounding speech at low bit rates by searching a codebook for the optimal excitation pattern that, when passed through a linear prediction synthesis filter, produces a reconstructed speech signal closest to the original. The encoder analyzes the input speech with linear prediction to model the vocal tract, quantizes the LPC coefficients, and performs a perceptually-weighted mean-squared error search through a codebook of excitation vectors to find the best match. The decoder reconstructs speech from the transmitted codebook indices and LPC parameters. Parameters: (1) analysis frame size, 180 samples for 22.05 kHz; (2) codebook type (adaptive/pitch codebook + fixed/gain codebook); (3) LPC order, 10 for 8 kHz sampling; (4) bit allocation between LPC coefficients, pitch lag, and codebook indices. Persistence mechanism: standardized in ITU-T G.721 (32 kbit/s), G.728 (16 kbit/s LD-CELP), G.729 (8 kbit/s), embedded in GSM EFR and AMR standards, and implemented in virtually all mobile telephone speech codecs from the 1990s onward. e.g.: the 8 kbit/s CELP algorithm of ITU-T G.729 recommendation; the 13 kbit/s GSM enhanced full-rate codec; the 12.2 kbit/s adaptive multi-rate codec of 3GPP TS 26.073; the 15 kbit/s CELP variant in G.728 low-delay CELP [formal: excitatio codicum praedicatio linearis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: long-term-prediction
payload.scope: People made long-term prediction to remove the redundant pitch-periodicity in speech signals that linear prediction (which models only short-term spectral structure) cannot capture, enabling more efficient speech coding.

definition.body: Long-term prediction is a human-made analysis technique that removes speech pitch periodicity by predicting each sample from samples at a previous pitch period, complementing short-term prediction that models vocal tract resonances. The prediction filter uses a feedback loop with a delay line of length equal to the estimated pitch period P, so that the predicted sample equals a weighted combination of past samples spaced P samples apart. The residual after long-term prediction has reduced periodicity and is better suited for vector quantization in speech coders. Parameters: (1) pitch period P, estimated from the autocorrelation function peak at lag 40-120 samples (60-180 Hz for typical speech); (2) prediction coefficient, typically 0.6-0.8; (3) number of previous pitch periods used, usually one in basic LTP. Persistence mechanism: described in speech coding textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Perlsman and Schafer), implemented in ITU-T speech codec standards (G.721, G.728, G.729), and used in the excitation processing chain of CELP-family coders. e.g.: the long-term prediction stage in ITU-T G.721 ADPCM speech coding; the LTP analysis in the AAC audio coding standard for tonal content; the pitch removal in AMR-WB codec excitation processing; the LTP module in the ITU-T G.729 CSLP codec [formal: praedicatio longinquorum temporum | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lpc-residual
payload.scope: People made LPC residual analysis to extract the excitation signal from speech by removing the spectral envelope modeled by linear prediction coefficients, isolating pitch and voicing information for analysis and coding.

definition.body: LPC residual is a human-made speech signal obtained by passing speech through the inverse of a linear prediction synthesis filter, removing the spectral envelope to reveal the underlying excitation. The residual represents the glottal source for voiced speech (quasi-periodic pulses) or random noise for unvoiced speech, free from vocal tract coloration. It is computed by applying the prediction error filter A(z) = 1 - sum(a_i * z^(-i)) to the speech signal. Parameters: (1) LPC order, determining how much spectral content is removed; (2) analysis frame length; (3) pre-emphasis filter coefficient. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis tools (Praat, HTK, Kaldi), used in speech coding (CELP excitation search), and described in speech processing textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Proakis and Manolakis). e.g.: the LPC residual used in pitch detection by Kaldi's plp feature pipeline; the excitation signal in Praat's speech synthesis vocoder; the residual in the LPC analysis step of the HTK speech processing toolkit; the residual computation in Rabiner and Schafer's Digital Processing of Speech textbook example code [formal: residuum praedictionis coefficientium linearium | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: formant-frequencies
payload.scope: People made formant frequencies to quantify the resonant peaks of the vocal tract transfer function, providing measurable acoustic correlates of vowel identity and vocal tract shape for speech analysis and synthesis.

definition.body: Formant frequencies are a human-made set of spectral peak locations that characterize the resonant properties of the vocal tract filter in the source-filter model of speech production. Each formant frequency F_n (typically F1 through F4) corresponds to a resonant mode of the vocal tract, determined by its geometry and impedance. The first formant (F1) inversely correlates with vocal tract openness (height); the second (F2) correlates with front-back tongue position; the third (F3) with lip rounding and vocal tract length. Parameters: (1) number of formants tracked, typically 3-5; (2) search bandwidth for peak detection; (3) formant bandwidths. Persistence mechanism: encoded in vowel space diagrams in phonetics research, used in speech recognition front-ends (MFCC derivation), implemented in Praat and other speech analysis tools, and taught as the foundational acoustic correlate of vowel identity in phonetics textbooks. e.g.: the formant values in Peter Ladefoged's Vowels and Consonants textbook vowel charts; the F1-F4 extraction in Praat formant tracking algorithm; the formant-based vowel classification in acoustic phonetics by Lieberman; the formant parameters in Klatt's parameterized vowel synthesis [formal: formae frequentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: ltp-coding
payload.scope: People made long-term prediction coding to exploit pitch periodicity in speech by quantizing the excitation signal at pitch-period intervals, reducing the bit rate needed compared to short-term coding alone.

definition.body: LTP coding is a human-made speech coding technique that encodes speech by exploiting long-term pitch periodicity. The encoder computes the long-term prediction residual, quantizes the LTP prediction coefficient, and encodes the pitch period and excitation residual using a codebook. The decoder reconstructs the excitation using the transmitted pitch period and codebook indices, passing it through a synthesis filter with LPC coefficients to reproduce speech. Parameters: (1) pitch period range, 20-160 samples; (2) LTP codebook size; (3) bit allocation for pitch lag, gain, and residual codebook indices. Persistence mechanism: used in ITU-T G.721 ADPCM speech coding, ITU-T G.728 LD-CELP, ITU-T G.729 CS-ACELP, and ITU-T G.723.1 dual-rate codec; implemented in Kaldi and HTK speech processing toolkits. e.g.: the LTP stage in ITU-T G.728 low-delay CELP at 16 kbit/s; the LTP in ITU-T G.723.1 at 5.3/6.3 kbit/s; the LTP analysis in the Kaldi ASR toolkit excitation processing; the pitch LTP in AMR-WB speech codec [formal: codificatio praedictionis longinquorum temporum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: parametric-speech-synthesis
payload.scope: People made parametric speech synthesis to generate speech from compact model parameters rather than stored waveforms, achieving the lowest bit rates for speech coding and enabling voice transformation.

definition.body: Parametric speech synthesis is a human-made approach that generates speech from compact parametric models of the vocal tract (typically LPC coefficients) and excitation source (pitch period, voicing, energy), rather than from stored or coded waveform samples. The synthesizer implements a parametric all-pole filter driven by a parametric excitation generator, with parameters interpolated between frames. Unlike waveform coding, parametric synthesis decouples speech quality from bit rate at the cost of naturalness, enabling extremely low bit rates (2.4-16 kbit/s) at the expense of robotic quality. Parameters: (1) LPC order and frame rate; (2) excitation model type (pitch-synchronous pulses, noise, or hybrid CELP codebook); (3) parameter interpolation method. Persistence mechanism: used in ITU-T G.723.1, AMR, and G.729 speech codecs for mobile telephony; implemented in parametric speech synthesis tools in HTK and Kaldi; used in voice transformation and speaker cloning research. e.g.: the parametric synthesis in ITU-T G.723.1 at 5.3/6.3 kbit/s; the AMR parametric speech codec in 3GPP TS 26.171; the parametric vocoder in the CMU ARK Toolkit; the speech synthesis in G.729 CS-ACELP at 8 kbit/s [formal: vox parametricus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.note: The source-filter model is maintained for the sake of speech synthesis: its decomposition into excitation source and vocal tract filter provides the parameterization that makes parametric speech synthesis possible. The model's parameters (pitch, LPC coefficients, formant frequencies, energy) are the direct control surface of synthesis vocoders from the Klatt synthesizer to modern TTS systems. For whose sake: the model was invented and is sustained specifically to enable synthetic speech generation. Direction: model (servant) → synthesis task (beneficiary).

payload.name: pitch-synchronous-oversampling
payload.scope: People made pitch-synchronous oversampling to increase temporal resolution of speech analysis at pitch periods for high-quality vocoders and time-stretching.

definition.body: Pitch-synchronous oversampling is a human-made speech analysis technique that samples the speech waveform at a rate proportional to the instantaneous pitch period, oversampling the signal during low-pitch periods to preserve phase continuity and reduce aliasing in vocoder synthesis. The algorithm estimates the pitch period via autocorrelation, then resamples the waveform at an integer multiple of the pitch period, applying a window centered on each glottal closure instant. Parameters: (1) oversampling factor, typically 2-4×; (2) pitch period estimation method; (3) window type and length relative to pitch period. Persistence mechanism: used in high-quality vocoder implementations such as the WORLD vocoder, in phase vocoder time-stretching, and in speech synthesis research for natural prosody control. e.g.: the pitch-synchronous analysis in the WORLD vocoder for speech synthesis; the pitch-synchronous oversampling in phase-vocoder time-stretching; the PSOLA-based speech modification toolkit; the pitch-synchronous windowing in the Praat speech analysis software [formal: superpositio pitch-synchrona | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: glottal-inverse-filtering
payload.scope: A human-made speech analysis technique that estimates the glottal airflow waveform by inverting the vocal-tract transfer function under constraints derived from parametric glottal-flow waveform models.

definition.body: glottal-inverse-filtering is a human-made speech analysis technique that estimates the glottal airflow waveform by inverting the vocal-tract transfer function under constraints derived from parametric glottal-flow waveform models. The method differs from general inverse filtering by imposing time-domain constraints on the residual waveform — specifying parameters such as open quotient, closed quotient, and the functional form of the opening and closing phases — to ensure the output is a physically plausible glottal flow signal. The algorithm: (1) estimate the vocal-tract transfer function using linear prediction coefficients, (2) construct the inverse filter, (3) filter the speech signal, (4) iteratively optimize the glottal-flow model parameters (amplitude ratios, phase times, open/closed quotients) to minimize the error between the filtered residual and the model prediction. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform model family (Liljencrants-Fant, Rosenberg, KF, RSP); (2) the time-domain constraints (open quotient, closed quotient, opening/closing phase functions); (3) the optimization algorithm for model parameter estimation. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis software (Gimme software for LF-model inverse filtering, the STRAIGHT vocoder glottal source estimation, the Klatt synthesizer analysis module), used in clinical laryngology for voice-disorder diagnostics, and documented in speech science textbooks on voice analysis. e.g.: the Gimme software applying the Liljencrants-Fant model to constrain inverse filtering; the glottal source estimation in the STRAIGHT vocoder using the Rosenberg model; the KF model applied in the Klatt CSTR vocoder; the RSP model used in Praat voice analysis plugins for clinical diagnostics [formal: filtrum glottale inversum | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: excitation-model
payload.scope: A human-made parameterized description used in speech coding and synthesis to model the glottal excitation signal as a function of pitch period, voicing decision, and source characteristics — the model that specifies how to generate the excitation, not the signal itself.

definition.body: excitation-model is a human-made parameterized description used in speech coding and synthesis to characterize the glottal excitation signal. It specifies the excitation as a function of (1) pitch period or fundamental frequency, (2) voicing decision (voiced/unvoiced/transition), (3) source characteristics such as pulse shape, spectral tilt, or noise characteristics. The model is the set of parameters and rules that generate the excitation, distinct from the excitation-signal itself which is the actual time-domain waveform. Parameters: (1) fundamental frequency (F0) in Hz or pitch period in samples; (2) voicing label (voiced/unvoiced/silent) per frame; (3) source parameters (gain, spectral tilt, pulse amplitude, noise variance). Persistence mechanism: standardized in speech coding standards (ITU-T G.729, AMR, EVS) where excitation model parameters are quantized and transmitted; implemented in speech synthesis toolkits (HTK, Kaldi, STRAIGHT vocoder); documented in speech processing textbooks (Rabiner & Schafer, Stern & Yamada). e.g.: the CELP codebook-based excitation model in ITU-T G.729; the pitch-synchronous pulse excitation in ITU-T G.723.1; the ACELP random-codebook excitation in 3GPP AMR; the harmonic-plus-noise model in STRAIGHT vocoder excitation processing [formal: excitatio modelus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

[4 duplicate] The duplicate it alleges fails, and the direction is backwards. The two carves sit at different levels of specificity: the target carves the GENERAL family — 'searching a codebook for the optimal excitation pattern ... (2) codebook type (adaptive/pitch codebook + fixed/gain codebook)' — while acelp carves the SPECIFIC algebraic variant — 'sparse linear combination of codewords from an algebraic codebook ... sparse impulse positions, e.g., 4 pulses per subframe'. The target's own text refutes 'identical parameters and persistence': its persistence and examples include G.728 LD-CELP, the classic two-stage codebook with a fixed random-vector codebook, which is not algebraic and is outside acelp's carve. So acelp is a MEMBER of the CELP family, and the true relation runs acelp → code-excited-linear-prediction (instance/derivation), the reverse of the duplicate claim. Independent chronology confirms it: code-excited linear prediction (Atal & Schroeder, 1989) predates the algebraic codebook variant (Atal, 1991; ITU-T G.729) — the general term is the ancestor, not a reduplication of the descendant. A general family entry is not a duplicate of its specific member; the board's own specific-pipeline-not-a-duplicate-of-framework line runs the same way in reverse. The record stands: dismiss the contest.

payload.name: synthesis-filter
payload.scope: People made the synthesis filter to reconstruct speech waveforms from excitation samples and LPC coefficients in all-pole decoding, enabling real-time speech playback in compression and vocoder systems.

definition.body: A synthesis filter is a human-made all-pole digital reconstruction filter used in LPC-based speech coding and analysis systems. It reconstructs a speech waveform from a sequence of excitation samples and LPC coefficients. For a frame of excitation e(n) and p LPC coefficients a_k, the synthesis filter implements H(z) = G / (1 - Σ(a_k · z^(-k))) as a recursive difference equation: y(n) = Σ(a_k · y(n-k)) + G·e(n), where y is the output, G is the gain parameter, and a_k are the prediction coefficients. The filter is a stable all-pole IIR filter whose poles are determined by the LPC coefficients. Parameters: (1) prediction order p; (2) LPC coefficients a_1 through a_p; (3) gain G. Persistence mechanism: embedded in ITU-T G.729 CS-ACELP decoder; implemented in Kaldi and HTK synthesis toolkits; standard in AMR-WB and GSM speech codecs. e.g.: the synthesis filter in ITU-T G.729 CS-ACELP decoder stage; the LPC synthesis filter in Kaldi TTS vocoder; the G.723.1 decoder synthesis filter; the all-pole filter in Praat LPC analysis-synthesis pipeline [formal: filtrum synthesium | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-variance-normalization
payload.scope: People made cepstral variance normalization to equalize the spread of cepstral coefficients across speakers, removing inter-speaker variance mismatches that degrade speaker recognition and speech recognition performance.

definition.body: Cepstral variance normalization is a human-made signal processing technique that equalizes the variance of cepstral coefficient vectors across frames or speakers. It computes the variance per coefficient dimension across a dataset or utterance, then divides each frame's coefficients by the standard deviation to produce unit-variance features. Unlike mean normalization (which removes DC bias), variance normalization alone addresses spread differences caused by recording conditions, channel effects, or inter-speaker variability. Parameters: (1) the reference set over which variance is computed (single utterance, speaker corpus, or sliding window), (2) the per-dimension variance estimate, (3) optional floor value to prevent division by near-zero variance. Persistence mechanism: implemented in Kaldi and HTK speaker recognition pipelines; documented in speech processing toolboxes as a preprocessing step; standard in voice recognition front-ends. e.g.: the variance normalization in Kaldi speaker recognition recipe; the cepstral variance scaling in HTK speaker identification front-end; the per-dimension variance equalization in CMU ARK Toolkit; the variance normalization stage in VoxForge preprocessing | not: cepstral-mean-variance-normalization which jointly normalizes mean and variance; cepstral-mean-normalization which only removes the DC offset [formal: normalizatio cepstralis varientialis | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: pitch-lag
payload.scope: People made pitch lag as a numerical parameter representing the delay between consecutive pitch periods in speech coding, enabling long-term prediction and excitation reconstruction in CELP-based codec systems.

definition.body: Pitch lag is a human-made numerical parameter that encodes the delay between consecutive pitch periods in speech coding. It represents the time offset (in samples) at which the past excitation signal best matches the current excitation, used in long-term prediction (LTP) and codebook-excitation stages of speech codecs. The pitch lag L is computed as the delay that maximizes the normalized cross-correlation between the current excitation window and a past excitation window shifted by L samples: L = argmax_r Σ[n](x[n]·e[n-L]) / sqrt(Σ[n]x²[n]·Σ[n]e²[n-L]). Parameters: (1) the analysis frame or subframe; (2) the search range (typically 20-160 samples at 8kHz, corresponding to 62.5-250 Hz); (3) the resolution (integer, 1/3 fractional, or 1/6 fractional samples). Persistence mechanism: transmitted as a quantized index in speech codec bitstreams (ITU-T G.729 transmits 14-bit pitch lag per subframe; 3GPP AMR transmits pitch lag for adaptive codebook); implemented in Kaldi and HTK LTP analysis; documented in speech processing textbooks. e.g.: the 14-bit pitch lag index transmitted per subframe in ITU-T G.729 CS-ACELP; the fractional pitch lag in 3GPP AMR narrowband codec; the adaptive codebook gain and pitch lag in ITU-T G.723.1; the pitch lag search in Kaldi LTP encoder [formal: retardatio pitch | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: prewhitening
payload.scope: People made prewhitening to flatten the spectral tilt of speech signals before analysis, removing the natural -6 dB/octave roll-off to improve cepstral and LPC estimation accuracy.

definition.body: Prewhitening is a human-made signal preprocessing technique that flattens the spectral tilt of a signal before spectral analysis by passing it through the inverse of an estimated spectral envelope filter. In speech processing, the vocal tract imparts approximately -6 dB/octave spectral roll-off; prewhitening removes this by applying the prediction-error filter (the inverse of the LPC all-pole synthesis filter) to the input signal, producing a spectrally flat whitened residual. The procedure: (1) estimate the LPC coefficients a_k from the input speech frame; (2) construct the prediction-error filter A(z) = 1 - Σ(a_k·z^(-k)); (3) filter the input signal through A(z) to obtain the whitened residual. Parameters: (1) the analysis frame; (2) the LPC prediction order; (3) the pre-emphasis factor if applied before or after. Persistence mechanism: implemented in the Kaldi lpc_prewhitening utility; used in HTK cepstral feature extraction pipelines as the default pre-processing; documented in speech processing textbooks as standard practice for LPC analysis. e.g.: the Kaldi lpc_prewhitening function in the lcomputation toolkit; the HTK cepstral feature extraction prewhitening stage; the prediction-error filtering in Praat LPC analysis; the prewhitening step in the CMU ARK Toolkit cepstral feature computation | not: pre-emphasis (simple first-order high-pass, not LPC-based); spectral-whitening (spectrum equalization without LPC prediction-error filter) [formal: prae-albificatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-energy
payload.scope: A human-made scalar measure derived from the cepstrum, used to quantify periodicity in a signal by aggregating cepstral coefficients into a single energy value.

definition.body: Cepstrum-energy is a scalar measure computed from the cepstrum of a signal, typically as the sum of squared cepstral coefficients in a specified quefrency range. It quantifies the strength of periodic structure in the cepstral domain — higher cepstrum-energy at quefrencies corresponding to the pitch period indicates strong periodicity, while near-zero energy at those quefrencies indicates aperiodicity. Parameters: (1) the cepstral coefficients used (typically the first 12-24 coefficients); (2) the quefrency range of interest (e.g., 1-20 ms for speech pitch); (3) the aggregation method (L2 norm, sum of squares, or weighted sum). Persistence mechanism: used in pitch detection algorithms, voicing decision systems, and periodicity measurement in speech processing toolkits and research implementations. e.g.: L2 norm of cepstral coefficients 2-20 in Praat for voicing detection; sum of squared coefficients 3-15 in librosa for periodicity analysis; weighted cepstrum-energy in CMU Sphinx for Viterbi-based speech segmentation; energy at quefrency 5ms in Kaldi for speaker diarization | not: cepstral-coefficient (a single coefficient, not an aggregate energy measure); spectral-energy (energy in the frequency domain, not the cepstral domain) [formal: energia cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes]

payload.name: autocovariance
payload.scope: A statistical construct humans made to measure the covariance of a signal with its own lagged values, quantifying how data points at one time relate to data points at previous times without normalizing by variance.

definition.body: An autocovariance is a human-made statistical measure of the covariance between a time series and a lagged version of itself at lag k. It is computed as the average of the products of deviations from the mean: γ(k) = E[(X_t - μ)(X_{t-k} - μ)], where X_t is the time series, μ is the mean, and k is the lag. Unlike autocorrelation, autocovariance is not normalized — its magnitude depends on the signal's variance. Parameters: (1) the time series data, (2) the lag k (non-negative integer), (3) the estimator used (biased, unbiased, or consistent). Persistence mechanism: computed by statistical libraries (numpy, scipy, R), used as input to autocorrelation normalization (ρ(k) = γ(k)/γ(0)), and foundational to AR model identification via the Yule-Walker equations. e.g.: numpy.cov computation of lag-0 autocovariance for a financial return series; scipy.signal.correlate with mode='full' to compute autocovariance sequence; R's acf function with type='covariance' to estimate autocovariance at multiple lags | not: autocorrelation; cross-covariance [formal: autocovariantia | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-decorrelation
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing procedure that decorrelates cepstrum feature vectors by applying a linear transform to remove inter-coefficient redundancy for classification.

definition.body: Cepstrum-decorrelation is a human-made signal processing procedure that decorrelates cepstrum feature vectors to remove inter-coefficient redundancy for classification. It applies a linear transform to the cepstral coefficients such that the output covariance matrix is diagonal. Parameters: (1) the input cepstral feature matrix (frames × coefficients), (2) the training data for computing the covariance/eigenvectors, (3) the number of retained principal components. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech recognition front-ends as a preprocessing step. e.g.: Kaldi transform_feats.py with PCA decorrelation on MFCC features; HTK DCT cepstral normalization applied before delta-delta computation; NIST SRE i-vector extraction with PCA-decorrelated cepstral features | not: cepstral-decorrelation (the statistical property of reduced coefficient correlation, not an active procedure); cepstrum-smoothing (low-pass filtering that preserves envelope structure) [formal: decorrelatio cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstrum-subband
payload.scope: A human-made signal processing technique that partitions the cepstrum into contiguous quefrency subbands for independent processing and feature extraction.

definition.body: Cepstrum-subband is a human-made signal processing technique that partitions the cepstrum into contiguous subbands in the quefrency domain, processing each subband independently for analysis or feature extraction. The procedure: divide the quefrency range of the cepstrum into M contiguous subbands (typically M=3-8), optionally apply different processing (filtering, normalization, statistics) to each subband, then optionally combine subband outputs. Parameters: (1) the input cepstrum, (2) the subband partition scheme (uniform, perceptually-mapped, or adaptive), (3) per-subband processing operations. Persistence mechanism: used in cepstrum-based signal classification, speaker identification, and audio segmentation systems where subband processing provides robustness against quefrency-domain noise and channel effects. e.g.: subband cepstrum processing in Kaldi's cepstrum-based voice activity detection; subband cepstrum analysis in HTK for speaker-independent phoneme recognition; subband cepstral features in NIST speaker verification with adaptive quefrency partitioning | not: cepstrum-smoothing (applies uniform low-pass filtering across the entire cepstrum, not subband partitioning); cepstral-subband (operates on cepstral coefficients in index space, not cepstrum in quefrency space) [formal: divisio-cepstralis subbando | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-mean
payload.scope: A scalar computed as the arithmetic mean of cepstral coefficients over a defined set, serving as a baseline for spectral normalization.

definition.body: Cepstral-mean is a scalar computed as the arithmetic mean of a set of cepstral coefficients, typically over a single analysis frame or a short window of frames. It captures the overall spectral level across the cepstral dimensions and serves as a baseline for normalization procedures. Parameters: (1) the set of cepstral coefficients to average (e.g., coefficients 0-12 of an MFCC vector); (2) the aggregation scope - a single frame or a sliding window of consecutive frames. Persistence mechanism: computed as part of cepstral-mean-normalization pipelines in Kaldi, HTK, and CMU Sphinx feature extraction toolkits; stored as a scalar feature in speech processing databases. e.g.: the mean of the first 13 MFCC coefficients per frame in Kaldi compute-cmvn-stats; the frame-level cepstral mean in HTK HTKTool feature extraction; the per-utterance cepstral-mean feature in the TIMIT acoustic-phonetic corpus | not: cepstral-mean-normalization (a procedure that subtracts this value, not the value itself); cepstral-coefficient (a single value, not an aggregate) [formal: media cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-zeroth-coefficient
payload.scope: A cepstral coefficient at index zero, equal to the logarithm of the signal energy, serving as a measure of spectral energy level in the cepstral domain.

definition.body: Cepstral-zeroth-coefficient is the cepstral coefficient at index zero (c[0]), equal to the natural logarithm of the sum of squared signal samples (log-energy). It captures the overall energy of the signal in the cepstral domain and is used as a feature for voice activity detection, speaker recognition, and signal-to-noise estimation. Computation: c[0] = (1/N) * Σ log(x[n]²) over the analysis frame of N samples, where x[n] is the windowed speech signal. Parameters: (1) the analysis frame samples; (2) the normalization factor (1/N for mean energy, or 1 for total energy). Persistence mechanism: computed in voice activity detection frontends, stored as a feature in speaker recognition databases, and used in SNR estimation routines in Kaldi, HTK, and MATLAB speech processing toolkits. e.g.: the log-energy feature extracted in Kaldi compute-vadstats; the c[0] value in HTK HTKTool for energy-based voice activity detection; the cepstral DC component used in MATLAB voicebox for energy-based voiced/unvoiced classification | not: cepstral-coefficient (a general class of coefficients, not the specific index-zero value); rms-energy (energy in the time/frequency domain, not the cepstral-domain log-energy at index zero) [formal: coefficientes-cepstralis zero | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: periodicity-measurement
payload.scope: People made periodicity measurement to quantify the strength of the repeating structure in a signal — how periodic it is — without committing to a specific fundamental-frequency value, so frames can be routed to pitched or unpitched processing and voice and room quality can be graded on the periodic component alone.

definition.body: Periodicity-measurement is a family of quantitative constructs that measure the strength of the periodic structure present in a signal, independent of the fundamental-frequency value that pitch estimation reports. It answers how periodic a signal is rather than what its pitch is. Parameters: (1) the periodicity statistic — the normalized autocorrelation peak height at the dominant lag, the cepstral peak side, the periodic-to-aperiodic (P2A) energy ratio, or the harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR); (2) the analysis frame and the lag or quefrency search range bounded by the plausible period; (3) the output scale — a unitless ratio or a decibel measure. Persistence mechanism: implemented in voice-quality and speech toolkits (the CPS, P2A and HNR features), in voiced/unvoiced classifiers, and in audio coding and source separation, where a periodicity score routes frames to pitched or unpitched models. e.g.: the cepstral peak side (CPS) feature in voice quality analysis; the periodic-to-aperiodic (P2A) energy ratio in voice quality assessment; the harmonic-to-noise ratio (HNR) in voice quality; the height of the normalized autocorrelation peak used as a periodicity index in voiced/unvoiced classification | not: pitch-estimation (reports the F0 value, not the degree of periodicity); voicing-decision (a binary voiced/unvoiced label, not a graded score); spectral-energy (a level measure with no periodicity content) [formal: mensura periodicitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: adpcm
payload.scope: People made adaptive differential pulse-code modulation to carry voice at a fixed low bit rate by quantizing only the prediction error of an adaptive predictor instead of the full sample, so the quantizer can spend its bits where the signal is least predictable.

definition.body: Adaptive differential pulse-code modulation (ADPCM) is a human-made predictive waveform-coding procedure that encodes the error between a speech sample and its adaptive prediction rather than the sample itself. Procedure: (1) an adaptive linear predictor forms the prediction from past samples (G.726 keeps a 16-coefficient predictor whose coefficients adapt to the local signal); (2) the difference between the actual sample and the prediction, the prediction error, is quantized by a log-law quantizer whose step size adapts to the signal level; (3) the quantized error index and the step-size index are transmitted as a fixed-rate code word, and the receiver reconstructs the sample as prediction plus quantized error. Parameters: (1) the bit rate, 16, 24, 32 or 40 kbit/s in ITU-T G.726; (2) the predictor order, 16 in G.726; (3) the quantizer structure, a 64-entry log-law quantizer with an adaptive step size. Persistence mechanism: specified in ITU-T G.726 (1988, reaffirmed), implemented in ISDN voice channels and conference-bridge and audio-conferencing codecs, and described in the speech-coding literature as the canonical low-rate predictive codec. e.g.: the G.726 24 kbit/s codec as an ISDN voice channel; the G.726 32 kbit/s codec in an E1/T1 digital voice path; the G.726 40 kbit/s codec at full duplex voice rate | not: pure delta modulation (1-bit per sample with no multi-bit prediction-error quantization); sigma-delta modulation (1-bit oversampled feedback stream); pulse-code-modulation (encodes the full sample with no prediction stage) [formal: modulatio differentialis adaptiva | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Law 7, independent chronology. Pulse-code-modulation is the standing ancestor: the PCM procedure (sample, quantize, code the full sample) is the fixed-rate digital voice codec ITU-T G.711 specifies for 3.1 kHz speech, and ADPCM is the differential refinement of it - the 1988 ITU-T G.726 standard keeps the PCM rate law (samples at the Nyquist rate, fixed bits per sample) while moving the quantizer onto the prediction error of an adaptive predictor. The later construct (ADPCM, G.726 1988) points to what it came from (PCM, G.711 lineage): PCM stood first and fed into ADPCM, and PCM operates without ADPCM (the full-sample codec is complete on its own), so this is lineage, not dependence. Not a simultaneous pair: the two standards are decades apart, and the derivation is stated from the standards' own history, not from the graph's epoch.

payload.name: scalar-quantization
payload.scope: People made scalar quantization to carry a continuous-amplitude signal on a fixed number of bits per sample by mapping each single sample value to the nearest member of a finite level set.

definition.body: Scalar quantization is a human-made procedure that maps a single continuous amplitude value to the nearest level of a finite discrete level set, so a signal can be carried on a fixed number of bits per sample. The quantizer partitions the amplitude range into intervals and assigns each interval an index; the decoder returns the level index as the reconstructed amplitude. Parameters: (1) the number of levels, 2 to the b for a b-bit quantizer; (2) the level law - uniform levels at fixed spacing, or non-uniform log-law levels denser near zero; (3) the level placement, midrise with zero as a level, or midtread with zero as an interval midpoint; (4) the step size and the overflow range beyond the outermost level. Persistence mechanism: specified in ITU-T G.711 (mu-law and a-law 8-bit log-law quantizers), ITU-T G.726 (64-level log-law quantizer), and the CD Red Book (16-bit uniform quantization), and described in the quantization literature (Gray and Neuman, 1966) as the foundational block of every fixed-bit-rate waveform coder. e.g.: the 8-bit mu-law quantizer of ITU-T G.711 T1 voice; the 16-bit uniform quantization of a 44.1 kHz Red Book CD track; the 64-level log-law quantizer of ITU-T G.726 ADPCM | not: vector-quantization (maps a vector to a codebook prototype, not a single value); delta modulation (encodes the signal difference with one bit, not the sample amplitude); model quantization of float32 weights to int8 (a computational precision reduction, not a signal coder) [formal: quantificatio scalaris | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

replacementSpec.body: Quantization is a human-made procedure for representing a continuous-amplitude signal or a continuous numeric range with a finite set of discrete levels, so the signal can be carried or computed with a fixed number of bits. The procedure partitions the input range into intervals and assigns each interval an index and a reconstruction value; the quantizer maps an input value to the nearest reconstruction value, and the decoder emits that value. Parameters: the number of levels, the level law, uniform or non-uniform, the level placement midrise or midtread, the step size and the overflow behavior. Persistence mechanism: sustained use in digital signal processing, audio coding, communications, and measurement, encoded in standards ITU-T G.711, ITU-T G.726, ISO/IEC 11172-3, and the CD Red Book, and described in the information theory literature (Shannon, Gray-Neumann). e.g.: the 8-bit mu-law quantizer of ITU-T G.711 T1 voice; the 16-bit uniform quantization of a Red Book CD track; the 64-level log-law quantizer of ITU-T G.726 ADPCM | not: dithering which adds noise to mask quantization artifacts; noise shaping which reshapes quantization noise spectrally; vector quantization which maps vectors not single values [formal: quantificatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]
